title: Scenarios iter-4: 72 pass, 45 weak, 3 fail
intro: The 40 everyday requests played against a fresh hub with GPT-6 Luna, 3 rep(s) each, a simulated non-technical person answering, judged by a model on each request's Good line. One item per case: give your own verdict and comment where the judge or the agent got it wrong. Total cost $4.606. The full report is .harness-test/scenarios/iter-4/report.md.

items.title: Diagnosis: what the model was shown, why it went that way, and the fixes ranked
items.ask: Are these the right fixes, in the right order? Which would you make first?
items.md:
# Diagnosis: iter-4

Written 2026-11-25T21:43:18.533Z by openai/gpt-6-luna from 119 case rep(s): what the chat model was shown at every step, and why it did what it did. Cost $1.031 (cases $1.013, merging $0.0180). Not diagnosed: 37/r3 (the model's JSON didn't fit 3 times: steps.1.why: Invalid option: expected one of "missing-info"|"misleading-info"|"jar…).

## Why each step went the way it did

| cause | steps |
|---|---|
| fine | 444 |
| model-error | 117 |
| tool-bug | 102 |
| wrong-mechanism | 47 |
| missing-info | 35 |
| misleading-info | 25 |
| mechanism-too-hard | 5 |
| mechanism-missing | 5 |

**Model arg mistakes** (the model's own call didn't fit and was sent back; not failures in themselves): 11 not recovered, 9 recovered.

## Fixes, ranked by how many case reps they would help

### 1. `hub-behaviour` — 15 case rep(s), confidence 0.77

From [1/r2](rep-2/cases/case-01.md), [1/r3](rep-3/cases/case-01.md), [10/r1](rep-1/cases/case-10.md), [10/r3](rep-3/cases/case-10.md), [11/r3](rep-3/cases/case-11.md), [12/r1](rep-1/cases/case-12.md), [12/r2](rep-2/cases/case-12.md), [12/r3](rep-3/cases/case-12.md), [21/r2](rep-2/cases/case-21.md), [27/r1](rep-1/cases/case-27.md), [27/r2](rep-2/cases/case-27.md), [27/r3](rep-3/cases/case-27.md), [34/r1](rep-1/cases/case-34.md), [34/r2](rep-2/cases/case-34.md), [34/r3](rep-3/cases/case-34.md).

**Problem:** A web-search provider’s plan, quota, or usage limit caused repeated failures, with unclear recovery guidance and no reliable fallback.

**Proposed:**

> When a web-search provider returns a plan, quota, or usage-limit error, mark that provider unavailable for the rest of the current turn and do not send further requests to it during that turn. If another independently configured live-search provider is available, try it and identify the source of any results; if it also fails or is unavailable, return a clear failure that preserves the provider’s reason and states that web search could not be completed. Include a reset time or retry guidance only when the provider supplies it. Do not imply that the assistant can change the provider’s plan or contact it on the person’s behalf. Do not present unverified claims or links as checked, or treat searches of saved resources as live public-web search. The assistant may use other sources already available, clearly distinguish what was and was not verified, or explain that searching is unavailable.

### 2. `hub-behaviour` — 10 case rep(s), confidence 0.92

From [7/r2](rep-2/cases/case-07.md), [9/r2](rep-2/cases/case-09.md), [9/r3](rep-3/cases/case-09.md), [17/r1](rep-1/cases/case-17.md), [17/r1](rep-1/cases/case-17.md), [17/r2](rep-2/cases/case-17.md), [20/r1](rep-1/cases/case-20.md), [20/r2](rep-2/cases/case-20.md), [20/r3](rep-3/cases/case-20.md), [37/r1](rep-1/cases/case-37.md), [40/r1](rep-1/cases/case-40.md).

**Problem:** Database query authoring and table-function generation misclassified structured inputs as prose, gave generic or misleading errors, and could not reliably validate, save, or run supported queries.

**Proposed:**

> Fix the database authoring and execution path so structured query objects remain structured through drafting, validation, saving, and execution. Accept the documented query shapes, including inserts with multiple rows, and use date-value syntax supported by the active database dialect. Apply consistent validation to generated and authored insert and select queries, including aggregate queries with date filters. Check each generated query before saving or returning it; do not return a generated function that fails its own validation. Never label structured input as prose or present an internal authoring failure as invalid caller input when the supplied arguments fit the tool’s schema. For invalid input, name the exact field or path, expected shape, unsupported expression, or malformed argument, and give a concrete correction. Preserve the underlying helper’s actual failure reason. If a generated function is stale, identify it as stale and direct the caller to the supported discovery and regeneration process; verify that a regenerated list function returns the current rows. Do not direct callers to an editing route unless that route is a supported repair. After repeated identical failures without an identified correction, stop retrying and return the specific blocker rather than asking for an unchanged retry or a reworded description.

### 3. `context:hub/memory` — 7 case rep(s), confidence 0.84

From [4/r1](rep-1/cases/case-04.md), [4/r2](rep-2/cases/case-04.md), [7/r3](rep-3/cases/case-07.md), [8/r3](rep-3/cases/case-08.md), [9/r1](rep-1/cases/case-09.md), [9/r3](rep-3/cases/case-09.md), [10/r1](rep-1/cases/case-10.md).

**Problem:** The memory guidance is not consistently applied: the assistant may fail to search for existing personal details, save newly shared durable facts from chat or forms, retain separate household or preference facts, or exclude temporary details and individual list or log entries.

**Proposed:**

> Before asking for a personal preference, limit, routine, household fact, or other detail, search saved memories with `hub__ctx_search` using `origins: ["memory"]`, unless relevant memories are already available in the conversation. When a person shares a lasting preference, goal, routine, limit, or other fact likely to help in a later chat, save it with `hub__remember` in the same step as the related work when practical. Apply this to form answers as well as ordinary messages. Use the appropriate scope, including `scope: "user"` for durable facts about the person or their household. Save each distinct durable fact as its own memory, in one plain sentence; if several preferences together form one concise fact, keep that fact in one sentence. Include lasting household facts, such as who is in the household or how many people plans should account for, when stated, but do not assume a fact is permanent unless the person's wording supports that. Do not infer unstated facts. Keep individual entries and entry-specific details in the system that stores a list, log, or database, not in memory. Do not save details that matter only to the current task or other temporary details.

### 4. `context:web/guide` — 6 case rep(s), confidence 0.86

From [1/r3](rep-3/cases/case-01.md), [10/r1](rep-1/cases/case-10.md), [10/r2](rep-2/cases/case-10.md), [11/r1](rep-1/cases/case-11.md), [21/r1](rep-1/cases/case-21.md), [27/r1](rep-1/cases/case-27.md).

**Problem:** The guidance does not adequately explain how to respond when public-web search itself fails, especially because of a provider limit, or how to choose a genuinely different fallback without claiming unsupported results.

**Proposed:**

> If `web__search` fails, treat the search as incomplete: it does not establish that no information or source exists. Read the error. If it reports a quota, usage-limit, plan-limit, service-unavailable, or similar provider error, do not retry the same provider with different words, filters, or search depth. Try at most one genuinely independent route, if available. You may read a relevant URL already supplied by the person or found in a source you have read, or check configured API services with `api__services` and use one only if a listed service or documented public endpoint fits. Follow the API guide and verify a successful result before saying the lookup works. Never invent a URL, service, or connection. If no route works, say plainly what failed and what you could not check; do not guess, present unverified changing details or links as facts, or promise a later lookup without an established working source. You may give clearly labeled general guidance, separate from verified facts, or suggest a relevant official source the person can check directly, making clear you have not checked it. If asked for a recommendation despite the limitation, give the clearest reasonable option, state its key assumption, and briefly identify what remains unverified.

### 5. `context:hub/saved_fns` — 4 case rep(s), confidence 0.90

From [2/r1](rep-1/cases/case-02.md), [2/r3](rep-3/cases/case-02.md), [5/r1](rep-1/cases/case-05.md), [17/r3](rep-3/cases/case-17.md).

**Problem:** Guidance for ongoing tracking did not clearly distinguish persistent structured storage from documents and memories, or make reusable entry and review workflows concrete. It also missed asking for required details and confirming before setting up a log.

**Proposed:**

> Choose storage based on what the person wants to do later. Use the files system for a readable document, note, or summary. For structured entries or fields they want to revisit and change over time, use a database table as the source of truth; do not substitute a Markdown file. A memory is a note for later, not a history of repeated entries. If a required detail is missing, say what you checked and ask the person for it. If their wording suggests they want to track repeated events or entries so they do not have to remember them, offer a reusable log, explain plainly what it would keep, and ask before setting it up. For ongoing tracking, make or reuse a persistent place for the entries. Chat entry is always an option; when repeated entry has several fields or would be easier as a guided flow, use the input system to make a reusable form. A form collects answers but does not store them in the persistent place, so save its answers to the database. When the person would benefit from returning to a list, chart, calendar, or other view, use the widgets system to propose a lasting view over a read-only function that returns the relevant rows. For totals or counts by a group, use or create a query that calculates the requested aggregation; do not use a count when the person needs a sum. A widget proposal is not saved until the person chooses Save. Do not create a form or widget when a simple one-time answer is enough, unless reuse would help.

### 6. `context:input/basics` — 4 case rep(s), confidence 0.88

From [2/r2](rep-2/cases/case-02.md), [3/r1](rep-1/cases/case-03.md), [3/r2](rep-2/cases/case-03.md), [17/r3](rep-3/cases/case-17.md).

**Problem:** The guidance explains forms but does not clearly recommend them for repeatable, multi-field entry or distinguish collecting answers from saving them, so the assistant may default to chat and leave the storage step unclear.

**Proposed:**

> When someone wants to add entries repeatedly, or wants the same set of typed fields available to fill in again, consider a saved form if it would make each entry quicker or more consistent. Use `input__get_input` (also referred to as `input/get_input`) to create or reuse a form, including only the fields needed for one entry and indicating which are required. Chat messages remain an option, especially for a one-off entry or when the person prefers chat. A form collects answers; it does not store them or change stored data. After the person submits the form and the answers arrive, use the appropriate storage system to save or update those values; if using a database, call its write function once for that submission. If the person wants the form ready for later rather than filled in now, explain how to open it again. After showing a form, end your turn and process the answers when they arrive.

### 7. `context:hub/attached_files` — 3 case rep(s), confidence 0.99

From [6/r1](rep-1/cases/case-06.md), [6/r2](rep-2/cases/case-06.md), [6/r3](rep-3/cases/case-06.md).

**Problem:** The attachment guidance requires a second confirmation before recording information, even when the person has clearly requested the action and the required details are readable.

**Proposed:**

> Read an attached picture or document before answering about it. When the person clearly asks you to take an action using the attachment, treat that request as authorization and proceed with the details that are clear and required; do not ask them to confirm those details again. Ask only about a required detail that is missing, unreadable, uncertain, or genuinely ambiguous and cannot safely be resolved. If only one part of the task depends on an unclear detail, complete the parts that do not depend on it and ask a concise question about that detail. Ask about a category or other destination requirement if it is needed to complete the action; do not let an unclear optional detail block the rest. If the person has not requested a change, describe what you can read and ask what they would like done before making the change. A tool’s approval step is separate from chat confirmation: wait for the tool result before saying the change is complete. Report only what the attachment and tool results support.

### 8. `context:web/guide` — 3 case rep(s), confidence 0.92

From [14/r1](rep-1/cases/case-14.md), [14/r2](rep-2/cases/case-14.md), [14/r3](rep-3/cases/case-14.md).

**Problem:** The guidance encourages searching first without accounting for cases where the person has already supplied the exact page URL they want inspected.

**Proposed:**

> If the person supplies the exact URL of a page they want you to use, read it directly with `web__read`; do not search for that same page first. Search first only when you need to find a page or other sources and no suitable URL was supplied. If a search fails but the person has supplied a relevant URL, try reading that URL directly. If the page cannot be read, state what failed and use another approach only if one is available. When citing the page, use its final URL and rely on text you actually read.

### 9. `context:api/guide` — 3 case rep(s), confidence 0.90

From [24/r2](rep-2/cases/case-24.md), [25/r1](rep-1/cases/case-25.md), [25/r2](rep-2/cases/case-25.md).

**Problem:** The guide risks overstating what an absent API service listing proves and giving unsupported account-connection or setup instructions.

**Proposed:**

> A connection is an account sign-in used by a service. If a tool result says a service needs a sign-in, report that fact. Give a setup screen, navigation path, or link only when a tool result or guide for this app provides it; otherwise say you cannot verify where or how the person can connect the account. An empty API-services list establishes only that no matching service is configured for the API system. It does not establish an admin setup process, an available connection screen or link, or that no other connected system or saved function can access the service. Search the available functions for the service and requested action before saying access is unavailable. State only what each check established; if you find no usable function, say that you have not found one rather than claiming no connection exists. Do not imply that access or edits are available until the service and its required connection are confirmed. For an ordinary task, do not ask for a base URL or other technical setup details; offer a simple manual alternative instead. Discuss a base URL only if the person specifically asks to set up an API integration or has already provided the URL and wants to proceed. Never imply that you can connect an account yourself.

### 10. `context:database/basics` — 3 case rep(s), confidence 0.87

From [17/r3](rep-3/cases/case-17.md), [20/r2](rep-2/cases/case-20.md), [23/r2](rep-2/cases/case-23.md).

**Problem:** The guidance does not clearly distinguish temporary tasks from persistent data workflows or provide a complete sequence for checking, creating, and using suitable database-backed data.

**Proposed:**

> Use a database table for information the person wants to retain and update over time; do not create a persistent table merely to collect temporary responses for a one-time task. For persistent structured data, first call `database__databases` to inspect available databases and tables, load this guide, and check for a suitable existing table or saved functions. Before creating a table, confirm that writes are supported and that usable ways to add, read, and update records can be generated or verified. If no suitable table exists, create one with `database__create_table` and generate the needed ready-made functions with `database__table_fns_generate`, following the guide for exact arguments and approvals. Store the information as records, with fields for the state that needs to be tracked; represent separately updateable items or occurrences as separate data where needed. Use the functions to add, list, and update records. For any lasting view, use a read query or function that returns the table as its source; a document showing a snapshot is not a substitute for updateable data. If a function search result has a low similarity score and its description does not fit, reject it and search for the needed data operation. If required actions cannot be generated or verified, stop, explain what failed, and offer a working chat- or form-based alternative if appropriate. A printable or display document may be an additional format, but it does not replace the stored, updateable data.

### 11. `context:hub/later` — 3 case rep(s), confidence 0.87

From [26/r1](rep-1/cases/case-26.md), [26/r2](rep-2/cases/case-26.md), [26/r3](rep-3/cases/case-26.md).

**Problem:** The assistant explains that it cannot act later but may stop without helping with the request now. Guidance needs to require checking accessible information, asking for missing details when needed, and offering a reusable way to ask again without implying access to unconnected systems.

**Proposed:**

> When someone asks for something to happen later or repeatedly, explain plainly that this chat cannot run tasks or send messages automatically at a future time. Then help with what can be done now: check relevant information you can actually access, including the person’s saved memories when relevant, and provide a useful result from the sources checked. Use only systems and tools explicitly available in this chat; for example, use a calendar only if a calendar system is listed as available. Do not imply that you checked a source unless you have evidence from an available tool. If a relevant source is unavailable, say so plainly. If details are missing, do what you can without guessing and ask one short, specific question now about what is needed to finish the request. You may offer to save a simple reusable request, such as a `/command` using the memory tool if available. Make it broad enough to use relevant information available when the person asks again, rather than relying only on the current chat, and to disclose sources it cannot access. Suggest a reminder in the person’s own reminder or calendar app when helpful, but never claim that you set one or that a future task or message was scheduled.

### 12. `hub-behaviour` — 3 case rep(s), confidence 0.87

From [9/r2](rep-2/cases/case-09.md), [20/r1](rep-1/cases/case-20.md), [22/r2](rep-2/cases/case-22.md).

**Problem:** Function discovery returned no usable function names or signatures, sometimes showing only an unexplained count of additional results, leaving the model to guess what could be generated.

**Proposed:**

> Make function discovery return usable function names, signatures, and brief descriptions of their purpose in its first result, including standard add and list functions and whether each function already exists. For a newly created data structure, provide the ready-made functions that can be generated from its schema, and ensure the generation operation can create them. If results are paged, include a clear continuation token and instructions for requesting the next page. Do not return an empty list with a nonzero remaining-count field but no way to continue; if no functions are available, explain why.

### 13. `system-prompt` — 3 case rep(s), confidence 0.87

From [3/r3](rep-3/cases/case-03.md), [5/r2](rep-2/cases/case-05.md), [5/r3](rep-3/cases/case-05.md).

**Problem:** The assistant does not consistently recognize requests for repeated tracking, distinguish logs from memories, or set up a practical process for collecting entries.

**Proposed:**

> Treat a person’s difficulty remembering repeated events, dates, statuses, or other changing details as a possible request to track them over time. Check for an existing log first. If none exists, explain what a log would keep and offer to start one; ask for missing essential details before saving an entry. Use a database table or another suitable place that stores entries, not memory as a substitute for a history. Use memory only for a separate lasting fact or preference, and do not create a log when the person wants only one fact remembered. For repeated entries with multiple typed values, prefer a saved form over relying only on free-text chat. A form collects answers but does not store them: save confirmed answers to the log after submission, explain how to show the form again, and do not imply entries will be collected automatically. If creating the log requires approval, explain the proposed change and wait for approval; do not say it exists or save an entry until a tool result confirms the change.

### 14. `context:input/basics` — 3 case rep(s), confidence 0.84

From [7/r1](rep-1/cases/case-07.md), [7/r3](rep-3/cases/case-07.md), [23/r2](rep-2/cases/case-23.md).

**Problem:** The guidance does not sufficiently direct the assistant to gather several essential details together in a form when those details are needed to give a useful personalized response.

**Proposed:**

> When a useful response depends on two or more facts that only the person can provide, use `input__get_input` to ask for the essential details together as fields, especially before preparing a personalized recommendation or plan. Ask only for details that could materially change the first useful response; follow up later if needed. Describe each field and indicate whether it is required or optional. Ask one quick, informal question in chat instead when a form would add needless effort or the person prefers chat. After showing a form, end your turn and use the answers when they arrive.

### 15. `system-prompt` — 3 case rep(s), confidence 0.80

From [13/r1](rep-1/cases/case-13.md), [13/r2](rep-2/cases/case-13.md), [13/r3](rep-3/cases/case-13.md).

**Problem:** The assistant may omit a useful optional tone alternative when drafting a sensitive or potentially awkward message.

**Proposed:**

> When drafting a message, provide the version in the tone the person asked for first. For a sensitive or potentially awkward concern, briefly offer or include one alternative tone when it would be useful. Do not add alternatives when the person asks for only one version or when they would distract from the request.

### 16. `context:hub/limits` — 2 case rep(s), confidence 0.95

From [35/r1](rep-1/cases/case-35.md), [35/r2](rep-2/cases/case-35.md).

**Problem:** The guidance did not distinguish permission to create something from the method used to access it, or make clear that adding an item does not necessarily notify anyone or provide access. It also left room to infer an access method from unrelated permissions, mistake a system-connection token for a human-access credential, or invent unavailable setup steps.

**Proposed:**

> For any workflow, distinguish permission to create something from the method used to access it. A tool that adds a record does not, by itself, send a notification or invitation, provide a link or credential, or establish an access method. Do not present a token used to connect systems as a way for a person to access something. Do not infer the current access method from creation permissions or permissions governing tool use. After checking the relevant available functions, state plainly if they cannot show or change the current access method, send invitations, or set or reset credentials. Do not invent a link, credential, or settings path; offer a practical next step instead.

### 17. `hub-behaviour` — 2 case rep(s), confidence 0.93

From [22/r2](rep-2/cases/case-22.md), [36/r1](rep-1/cases/case-36.md).

**Problem:** Missing tool output left the agent unable to continue, and an unresolved call could be replayed on later turns without recovery or a usable final response.

**Proposed:**

> When a tool call has no matching output, return a structured error to the agent rather than leaving a dangling call or empty response. Check run and approval records for a completed result; if one exists, attach it so the agent can continue. If none exists, clear the stale call, report the actual failure once, and allow a fresh call or another recovery path on a later turn. Do not replay the same unresolved call or repeat the same missing-output error without attempting recovery. Let the agent provide verified partial results and clearly state what could not be checked.

### 18. `new-mechanism` — 2 case rep(s), confidence 0.92

From [36/r1](rep-1/cases/case-36.md), [36/r2](rep-2/cases/case-36.md).

**Problem:** Policy rules cannot be applied comprehensively to groups of functions by declared effects or modes, making broad coverage laborious and leaving future matching functions uncovered.

**Proposed:**

> Extend policy targets to support matching registered function effects and a `mode` field with the same values as function modes (`read`, `write`, and `delete`). Enforce these matches in the policy evaluator and describe them in the tool schema. A policy targeting a mode must match every function with that declared mode, including functions added later, without matching other modes. Before saving, preview every function that would be affected, identify functions with unknown or unclassified effects, and do not imply complete coverage when effects are unknown. Also allow multiple function-specific rules to be proposed and reviewed together.

### 19. `tool-description:web/read` — 2 case rep(s), confidence 0.91

From [1/r2](rep-2/cases/case-01.md), [12/r2](rep-2/cases/case-12.md).

**Problem:** The assistant guessed or constructed URLs and retried URLs after a 404, despite instructions to use established source URLs.

**Proposed:**

> Read a page only at a URL supplied by the person, returned by a search result, or linked to or identified by a page you have read. Do not guess or construct URLs from memory. A 404 or 410 means that URL has no readable page: never retry it, including with `render: "always"`. Use a different verified URL if one is available. If no source URL can be established or read, say so rather than trying a guessed address. For errors other than 404 or 410, follow the error's advice or try a different source.

### 20. `context:input/basics` — 2 case rep(s), confidence 0.90

From [20/r2](rep-2/cases/case-20.md), [20/r3](rep-3/cases/case-20.md).

**Problem:** The form guidance does not explain the limits of collecting responses from multiple people through one chat, or how to tally responses without promising shared access or automatic storage.

**Proposed:**

> For a one-time collection, use a form when fixed choices or several fields make it easier than a plain chat reply. A form collects answers only from the person who submits it in this chat; it does not create a shared link, give other people access, collect separate submissions from their accounts, save answers, or update a shared total. Do not promise these abilities unless an installed tool explicitly provides them. If several people are contributing through the same chat or device and their identities and number are known, one form may include a required choice field for each person. If those details are not known, ask only for what is missing, or use a form with a participant-identifier field and a choice field, presenting it again as needed. You may also offer a relay workflow: have the requester submit or relay each response in this chat, then summarize or count the responses shown here and state any tie. Explain that this is not a shared live poll and that the form does not store the answers. The requester may send responses in chat instead, and you can tally them. Use a database or other appropriate storage system for an ongoing history the person wants to keep, not merely because several responses are involved.

### 21. `hub-behaviour` — 2 case rep(s), confidence 0.90

From [23/r3](rep-3/cases/case-23.md), [40/r2](rep-2/cases/case-40.md).

**Problem:** Form enum validation could reject a displayed choice because typed aliases or display labels were not reliably converted to the canonical value expected by validation.

**Proposed:**

> For enum fields in forms, show the allowed values as selectable choices whenever possible. Ensure every displayed option submits successfully by submitting its canonical key or normalizing its display label to that key before validation and storage. If typed answers are allowed, accept exact choices and configured aliases, then normalize them to the canonical value. If an answer is not recognized, show the allowed choices and let the person correct it. Test enums with distinct keys and labels by rendering them, selecting each displayed option, and confirming each answer is accepted.

### 22. `suggestions` — 2 case rep(s), confidence 0.90

From [35/r1](rep-1/cases/case-35.md), [35/r2](rep-2/cases/case-35.md).

**Problem:** A function for connecting software components was suggested for a request to give an additional individual access, risking confusion between account access and establishing a connection.

**Proposed:**

> For a request to give an additional individual access, suggest the function for creating or inviting an account. Do not suggest a function for connecting separate software components for that request; suggest that function only when the request explicitly asks to establish such a connection.

### 23. `system-prompt` — 2 case rep(s), confidence 0.90

From [12/r1](rep-1/cases/case-12.md), [12/r2](rep-2/cases/case-12.md).

**Problem:** The assistant may cite remembered, unread, or truncated source material as though it verified a claim.

**Proposed:**

> For a factual claim you present as checked or sourced, cite only a URL returned by a tool or provided by the person, and only after you have read the relevant page. Do not present a URL from memory as a source you used. A citation to a page does not prove that it supports every claim: the relevant fact must appear in text you actually received and read. If a result is truncated before the relevant passage, read the remaining section before relying on it; if you cannot, say you could not verify the claim from that source. If a search or page read fails, say what you could not verify and do not attach an unverified link. Keep general knowledge distinct from facts confirmed in a source.

### 24. `system-prompt` — 2 case rep(s), confidence 0.90

From [13/r1](rep-1/cases/case-13.md), [13/r3](rep-3/cases/case-13.md).

**Problem:** Drafted first-person messages may contain unsupported claims about the person’s feelings, experiences, intentions, or the effects of an event.

**Proposed:**

> When drafting words for the person to send or say, use only facts and personal experiences they provided. Do not invent what they felt, noticed, experienced, intended, or what happened as a result. If a useful detail is unknown, leave it out, use a clear placeholder, or ask if it matters. Use neutral wording rather than making an unsupported first-person claim.

### 25. `system-prompt` — 2 case rep(s), confidence 0.90

From [18/r1](rep-1/cases/case-18.md), [18/r3](rep-3/cases/case-18.md).

**Problem:** When essential information is missing, the assistant may fail to offer an attached document as an optional way to provide it.

**Proposed:**

> When you need information only the person has and cannot find it in available data, say what you checked and ask for the essential details. Offer easy ways to provide them: the person can type or paste the key information, or attach a relevant document or image if it contains what is needed. Present an attachment as an option, not a requirement. Do not imply you can access a file unless it has been shared; read an attached document before relying on its contents. Ask only for information that matters, and for sensitive documents suggest omitting or covering details that are not needed.

### 26. `system-prompt` — 2 case rep(s), confidence 0.90

From [19/r3](rep-3/cases/case-19.md), [40/r1](rep-1/cases/case-40.md).

**Problem:** The assistant may claim a capability is unavailable based on checking only one system or source.

**Proposed:**

> Do not infer that the whole app cannot do something from one system’s limitation. Before saying a source, connection, or capability is unavailable, check the relevant available tools and services, including other systems that may provide it. State what you checked and what the results showed. Do not make a negative claim based on only one kind of source when another relevant system has not been checked; a later check does not support a claim made before that check.

### 27. `system-prompt` — 2 case rep(s), confidence 0.90

From [34/r1](rep-1/cases/case-34.md), [34/r3](rep-3/cases/case-34.md).

**Problem:** The assistant may replace a specific tool failure with a broader claim or provide unsupported links and exact instructions.

**Proposed:**

> When a tool fails, describe the reason it returned and say clearly what you could not check; do not replace a specific reason, such as a usage limit, with a broader claim. For exact app instructions, current screen labels, menu paths, or URLs, give specifics only when a tool result or guide in this chat supports them. Give a clickable link only if the person supplied it or a tool result showed that exact URL; do not guess or reconstruct URLs. If a lookup fails or is unavailable, say you could not verify the steps rather than filling in a likely path from memory. You may offer general knowledge or safety advice, clearly separated from verified information.

### 28. `context:web/guide` — 2 case rep(s), confidence 0.88

From [12/r1](rep-1/cases/case-12.md), [27/r3](rep-3/cases/case-27.md).

**Problem:** The guidance does not clearly distinguish live public-web search from searches of saved resources, allowing private or outdated saved material to be used as a fallback for current public information.

**Proposed:**

> A saved-resource search finds material already kept in the hub; it is not a live public-web search and may include the person's private files. Do not use it as a substitute when public-web search fails unless the person asks you to search saved material or you know a relevant public page was previously saved. Do not search the person's files unless the request calls for them. If live search fails, report that you could not verify sources, and do not present saved or old material as current. Provide only clearly labeled general information if no current source is available.

### 29. `system-prompt` — 2 case rep(s), confidence 0.88

From [30/r1](rep-1/cases/case-30.md), [35/r1](rep-1/cases/case-35.md).

**Problem:** The assistant may call a tool that changes information before telling the person what it will do.

**Proposed:**

> Before every function call that will add, change, or remove something, first tell the person in plain language what you are about to do, even when they requested the change. If the call needs approval, say that an approval request will appear. Then make the call and only confirm completion after the result says it succeeded.

### 30. `systems-list` — 2 case rep(s), confidence 0.87

From [22/r1](rep-1/cases/case-22.md), [22/r2](rep-2/cases/case-22.md).

**Problem:** The code system is described mainly as a tool for calculations and reshaping lists, obscuring its role in repeatable processing of uploaded files and its limits around storage and automatic execution.

**Proposed:**

> Code programs are saved pieces of logic that take inputs and return results; they do not store a person's data. For a repeated task involving uploaded files, first inspect a representative upload using the hub's resource-reading tools. If the contents can be supplied as text or rows, use `code__make_code` to create a reusable program that accepts the extracted inputs and returns transformed results, such as rows or a summary. Read each new upload with the resource tools and call the saved program on its extracted contents. Run it on the current file now; creating the program alone is not the result. A code program does not watch for files, read uploads on its own, store data, or run later automatically—the person must provide each new upload in chat, and you must read and process it then. Use the database system separately only when the person wants extracted results retained and looked up over time; do not create a database just for a one-time result per upload.

### 31. `context:web/guide` — 2 case rep(s), confidence 0.85

From [11/r2](rep-2/cases/case-11.md), [11/r3](rep-3/cases/case-11.md).

**Problem:** The guidance does not consistently explain when a useful practical time estimate is permissible after a lookup fails, or how to distinguish an estimate from verified or live information.

**Proposed:**

For a practical plan, you may provide a cautious approximate time or range only when you can make a useful estimate from the information provided; label it clearly as an estimate, allow a reasonable safety margin, and do not imply it is a live or verified result. Do not invent a precise departure, journey, or arrival time or imply that you compared options without supporting evidence. Use the person's local time and date when stating a clock time. Keep changing facts, such as current conditions, availability, costs, or advisories, separate from the estimate. Suggest a practical way to obtain missing live information, such as checking the relevant provider's current estimate. If a useful estimate is not possible, ask for the missing information or say what remains uncertain.

items.md:
**Request:** "I keep forgetting what I spend on groceries. Can you help me keep track?"

**Good:** Sets up somewhere to log trips, makes adding one easy, offers a monthly view.

Mean 5.7/10 · same verdict every rep · $0.195

### rep 1: weak 5/10

The grocery log was created, the Kroger trip was recorded, and November’s total was correctly reported. But the setup omitted the expected input form and monthly-view widget, and the entry was accidentally added twice before the duplicate was removed.

- ✓ Created a persistent log with date, amount, store, and note fields.
- ✓ Explained that future trips can be added by sharing the date and amount.
- ✓ Reported the correct November total of $172.48 and disclosed the duplicate correction.
- ✗ Did not set up the expected input form or monthly-view widget.
- ✗ Made a duplicate entry and then needed to remove it.
- ✗ Used an excessive number of tool calls for a simple setup and total.

Cause **missed-capability**, layer **chat-prompt**. Fix: Use the available form and widget capabilities to make logging and viewing monthly totals straightforward, and verify an entry before retrying a write.

2 turns · 33 runs · 21 model calls · hub $0.0448 · person $0.0012 · 89s · ended: satisfied (The monthly grocery log is set up and the November total came back correctly as $172.48, which is what I wanted.)

**Diagnosis:** The main miss was not a lack of capability information: the prompt’s Input section says a saved form can be shown again for repeated entry, and the Widgets section says a widget is a lasting view to keep and revisit. Step 6 nevertheless offered only chat-based entry and on-demand totals, so the setup lacked the expected form and monthly view. At step 5, the generated `datePerMonth` function was described as counting rows per month, while the needed monthly spending view required sums. The duplicate came from step 9: after the first create call returned “1 row changed,” the model repeated the same write instead of checking or trusting the successful result.

- `context:hub/saved_fns` (0.88): The guidance says to give a way to add and see recurring entries, but does not make the choice of a reusable form and a lasting view concrete enough. The model generated a monthly count function rather than the monthly sum needed for a spending view.
  > For something a person wants to track over time, first make a persistent place for the entries if none fits. Give them an easy way to add entries: when several typed fields recur and a form would make entry easier, use the input system to save a form they can fill in again. A form only collects answers; use the data system to save those answers. If they want a view they can revisit, use the widgets system. A widget needs a read-only function that returns the right rows; for totals or counts by month or another group, first make or find a query that calculates those totals or counts. Do not substitute a query that only counts entries when the person needs amounts summed. A widget proposal is not saved until the person presses Save. For a one-time list or answer, do not create a form or wid…
- `context:database/guide` (0.94): The guide explains that writes happen after approval, but does not explicitly warn against repeating a write after a successful result. The same create call ran twice, creating a duplicate.
  > After a write call, read its result before doing anything else. If it says the change succeeded (for example, it reports one row changed and returns the new row), treat that write as complete and do not repeat the same call. Retry only when the result clearly says the write did not happen, and follow the result's instructions. If you are unsure whether a write happened, read the affected data to check before trying again.

Describe only the essential fields, such as a date, amount, category, or note. A form asks for answers but does not store them: after the person submits it, save the answers with the system that keeps the entries. Chat messages remain a valid way to add entries; offer the form as a convenient repeatable option, not as a requirement. If you show the form, end your turn and process the answers when they arrive.
- `tool-description:database/get_query` (0.83): The description says a new query is “run once,” which can make its authoring preview look like the final user-visible result. The chat guidance says the preview is only a trial and the saved fn must be called for the real result.

The author may show a sample preview while writing the query; that preview is not a substitute for running the saved query to get the result for the person. After this call returns the saved query's name, call that saved fn (or database__run_query with its name and args) when the person asked to see the data now. A read result is shown to the person as a table when the result says so. Search for a saved query first when needed. In `detailedDescription`, say which tables and rows to use, what columns or totals to return, any grouping and order, and which changing values should be parameters. Write operations wait for the person's approval; do not claim…
- `context:widgets/basics` (0.81): The prompt describes widgets as lasting views, but does not directly connect an ongoing log and a request to see its monthly summary with proposing a widget. The assistant stated a total instead of making the current view visible and reusable.
  > For information the person expects to revisit, a widget is a saved view of a table-returning fn. For an ongoing log, when the person wants a summary they can return to, use a query that already groups and calculates the requested totals as the widget source. Call `widgets__make_widget` with that source and `show: true` when they asked to see the view now. The call only proposes the widget; the person must press Save to keep it. Do not say it is saved until a result confirms that. A one-time request to see rows can instead be answered by running the relevant read fn, which displays its rows when the result says so. Use a widget when a lasting view is useful, not for every data request.

- `context:database/basics` (0.87): The database instructions encourage generating table functions but do not sufficiently discourage making every available helper up front. After generating a function, load that exact function before calling it, and use the arguments in its signature. Creating another row is not a substitute for editing the existing row.

**Request:** "Track my daughter's reading minutes every night and show me how she's doing."

**Good:** A quick way to log a night, a chart over time.

Mean 6.3/10 · verdicts differ · $0.310

### rep 1: pass 8/10

The assistant created and populated a persistent reading log, made “minutes for tonight” a quick logging phrase, and accurately summarized the entries against the 20-minute goal. It proposed a chart but was clear that it could not save it when the Save control was unavailable, then provided a useful list instead.

- ✓ Saved all three dated reading entries correctly.
- ✓ Set up a quick phrase for logging tonight’s minutes.
- ✓ Clearly explained the chart-saving limitation without claiming the chart was saved.
- ✓ Reported goal results and total minutes accurately.
- ✗ The chart remained only a proposal, so the user could not open a saved progress chart.
- ✗ Did not set up the requested input form.

4 turns · 45 runs · 29 model calls · hub $0.0744 · person $0.0013 · 123s · ended: satisfied (I got a clear summary of the logged nights and goal results, and the assistant was upfront that it couldn't save the chart itself, so there's nothing left to push for.)

**Diagnosis:** At step 1, the prompt already explained that forms can be saved and shown again, and that they can collect typed fields, but the assistant chose ordinary chat entry instead of setting up the requested repeatable logging form. At steps 16 and 25–27, the assistant treated the proposal’s Save control as the only saving route. Although `widgets/save_widget` was not in the initial tool list, the prompt explained that other fns can be found with `hub__fns_search`, and the user explicitly asked the assistant to save the chart; it should have searched rather than concluding it could not. The log entries and final goal summary were otherwise handled accurately.

- `context:input/basics` (0.82): The instructions explain forms but do not make the choice especially salient for recurring entry logging, so the assistant relied on “tell me each night” instead of creating a reusable entry form.
  > When someone wants to record entries repeatedly, consider a saved form if it would make each entry quicker or more consistent. Use `input/get_input` to make and save a form with only the fields needed for one entry; connect the answers to the appropriate system that stores the entries. A form asks for answers but does not store them by itself. After showing a form, end the turn and process its answers when they arrive.
- `tool-description:widgets/make_widget` (0.88): The description says the person keeps a proposal by pressing Save, which can make that sound like the only route. The hub also has `widgets/save_widget`, but the assistant did not search for it when explicitly asked to save the proposal.
  > This fn proposes a widget and does not save it. If the person asks you to save a proposed widget yourself, search for and load the widget-saving fn, then use it if available; do not assume the preview’s Save control is the only way to save. If you cannot find or use a saving fn, explain the actual limitation and do not claim the widget was saved.

items.ask: Is the judge right? What should it have done?
items.md:
**Request:** "Keep a list of the books I've read and tell me what I should read next."

**Good:** Starts the list, asks a few books to start from, gives suggestions with reasons.

Mean 7.3/10 · verdicts differ · $0.128

### rep 1: pass 8/10

The assistant created a book log, recorded all four titles with the stated reactions, remembered the reading preferences, and gave three relevant recommendations with quick reasons. The log was checked to avoid a duplicate, and the assistant was transparent about the approval steps.

- ✓ Recorded all four books and their reactions
- ✓ Saved reading preferences for future recommendations
- ✓ Gave three fitting picks with reasons
- ✓ Checked the log before adding titles

3 turns · 25 runs · 18 model calls · hub $0.0474 · person $0.0011 · 109s · ended: satisfied (My books are logged and I got three good picks with reasons, which is exactly what I asked for.)

**Diagnosis:** The assistant chose the right overall approach and completed the log, but at step 11 it copied individual book titles and reactions into memory despite the prompt saying “not each form answer or entry of a list (entries belong where they are kept).” At step 17 it added optional author and genre fields that the person had not supplied, contrary to the instruction “Never fill it in yourself” and its earlier promise to leave unspecified metadata blank. At step 18 it gave plausible recommendations from general knowledge; the prompt described web use for current or outside information and reviews, but did not clearly tell the model when to verify recommendations with web pages. The person was satisfied, and the final claims that the books were logged are backed by the database results.

- `context:hub/memory` (0.87): The existing instruction says not to remember list entries, but the assistant still saved each title and reaction alongside the lasting preferences.
  > When a person is building a list or log, keep its individual entries and entry-specific details in the system that stores the list, not in memory. Use memory for lasting general preferences, limits, routines, or goals that may help in later chats. For example, remember a general preference for concise notes, but do not copy each note from a task list into memory.
- `system-prompt` (0.78): The instruction not to fill in missing names or other details did not prevent the assistant from adding unrequested optional metadata, and it contradicted its earlier promise to leave unspecified fields blank.
  > When saving a person's record, use the values they supplied or confirmed. Leave optional fields blank when they did not provide them; do not add guessed or independently supplied details just because they seem likely or helpful. Keep any promise you made about which fields you will leave blank unless the person changes that instruction.
- `context:web` (0.72): The web guidance explains search and reading pages but does not say when external verification is useful for recommendations. The assistant supplied factual descriptions without using web results.
  > For recommendations, use the web when current information, reviews, or a page's description would materially help choose or explain the options. Search for relevant pages, read the best one or two, and base factual descriptions on what they say. If general knowledge is enough for a useful answer, you may answer without browsing, but do not claim or imply that you checked current descriptions or reviews.

### rep 2: pass 8/10

The assistant created a persistent book list, asked for the person’s reading history and preferences, and recorded all four books with their reactions. It gave relevant sci-fi and memoir recommendations with brief reasons; its initial “queued” wording was slightly confusing because the insert had already been approved and completed.

- ✓ Created a database table for the reading list and saved all four books with the stated reactions.
- ✓ Asked for books and preferences before making personalized recommendations.
- ✓ Offered fitting standalone sci-fi picks and a memoir option, each with a reason.
- ✗ Initially described the books as queued for approval even though they had already been added.

3 turns · 19 runs · 15 model calls · hub $0.0371 · person $0.0006 · 101s · ended: satisfied (The book list is saved and I got several sci-fi picks plus a memoir option, each with a short reason.)

**Diagnosis:** The main result was successful: the database table was created, the four entries were written, and the recommendations were relevant. The avoidable gaps were that at step 2 the model did not follow the memory instruction to search before asking about personal preferences, and at step 8 it did not follow the instruction to save lasting preferences with `hub__remember`. At step 14 it said the entries were “queued” despite the result showing “4 rows changed”; it should have reported the completed action. The final confirmation at step 15 was supported by the approval result.

- `context:hub/memory` (0.72): The memory guidance says to search before asking about personal details and to keep lasting preferences, but the model skipped both actions in this task.
  > Before asking the person for a personal preference, limit, routine, or other detail about themselves, search their memories with `hub__ctx_search` using `origins: ["memory"]`, unless relevant memories are already in front of you. When the person reveals a lasting preference, limit, routine, or goal, save it as a user memory with `hub__remember` in the same step as the other work. Do not save details that matter only to the current task or individual entries that belong in a list or database. If several lasting preferences form one concise fact, keep that fact in one plain sentence.
- `system-prompt` (0.80): The model described a completed write as pending, despite the result reporting rows changed. The prompt says not to claim a change before confirmation but could more explicitly require reporting a confirmed completion accurately.
  > For every write, use the actual result to determine its status. If the result says the change completed or reports rows affected, say it is done; do not call it queued, pending, or awaiting approval. Say it is awaiting approval only when the result shows that approval is still pending. If the result does not make the status clear, say what the result confirms and what remains uncertain.

items.title: 5. Furnace filter — pass/weak/pass
items.ask: Is the judge right? What should it have done?
items.md:
**Request:** "When did I last change the furnace filter? I never remember this stuff."

**Good:** Admits it doesn't know yet, offers to start a home-maintenance log, asks for the date.

Mean 7.7/10 · verdicts differ · $0.0998

### rep 1: pass 8/10

It honestly said it couldn’t find a change date, saved the date and filter schedule once provided, and calculated that the filter is due now. It was clear that it can’t send a future nudge and suggested setting one on a phone or calendar.

- ✓ Checked existing memory and house notes before answering
- ✓ Saved the user-provided date, filter size, and replacement interval to memory
- ✓ Calculated the next due date and plainly stated it cannot send reminders later
- ✗ Didn’t explicitly ask for the last-change date or offer to start a maintenance log in its first reply

Cause **didnt-ask**, layer **chat-prompt**. Fix: When no replacement date is found, ask when it was last changed and offer to keep a maintenance log.

3 turns · 6 runs · 7 model calls · hub $0.0126 · person $0.0006 · 39s · ended: satisfied (It told me the filter is due now and that it can't nudge me later, which is straight with me, so I'll just set a reminder on my phone.)

**Diagnosis:** At step 1, the model searched memories, functions, and files but did not use the available database inventory, despite the database instructions saying to check whether a table exists; it therefore had not checked every plausible source before answering. At step 4, the system prompt said, “When a detail is missing … ask for it” and said to make a place for entries when someone wants to keep track over time, but the model only reported that it could not find the date. It missed the direct follow-up and log offer the situation called for. The later memory save, due-date estimate, and limitation about future reminders were handled appropriately.

- `context:database/basics` (0.83): The model did not check the database for an existing dated record before concluding it had not found the date. The existing guidance and database tool description say to inspect available tables, but a task-oriented reminder could make this step harder to miss.
  > When someone asks what or when something happened in the past, check the places that could hold that history before saying you could not find it. For database records, call `database__databases` to see which tables exist; searching functions finds tools, not rows of data. If a relevant table exists, load this guide and use a read query to check it. In your answer, be precise about which sources you checked and what they showed.
- `context:hub/saved_fns` (0.91): The general advice to keep entries over time did not lead the model to ask for the missing date or offer a log when the person said they often forget.
  > When you cannot establish a date or other detail needed to answer a question, say what you checked and ask the person for that missing detail. If their wording also suggests they want to track repeated events or entries so they do not have to remember them, offer to start a reusable log. A database table keeps the entries; a memory is a note for later, not a history of repeated entries. Ask before setting up a new log, and explain plainly what you would keep.

### rep 2: weak 6/10

The assistant correctly admitted it didn’t know the original change date, saved the date once provided, calculated the next due date, and was clear that it couldn’t create or send reminders. But it saved the information only as memory rather than offering or starting the home-maintenance log described in the Good line.

- ✓ Clearly said no filter-change date was available in the records it found.
- ✓ Saved the user-provided date and three-month interval, then updated the saved date after the new filter was installed.
- ✓ Calculated the due dates correctly and plainly explained its reminder limitation.
- ✗ Didn’t explicitly ask for the last-change date or offer to start a home-maintenance log.
- ✗ Didn’t use the available database capability to create a structured maintenance record.

Cause **missed-capability**, layer **chat-prompt**. Fix: When a user wants to track maintenance, offer to create a log and save the confirmed date and interval in a structured database record as well as memory.

4 turns · 12 runs · 16 model calls · hub $0.0561 · person $0.0007 · 82s · ended: satisfied (I got the next due date and the saved change date, and I’ll handle the repeating reminder in my own calendar.)

**Diagnosis:** At step 10, the prompt said, “When a detail is missing… do the parts that don't depend on it, and ask for it,” and the tracking guidance said to offer a place to keep repeated entries; the assistant stopped after reporting the missing date. At step 11, it explicitly considered a database but dismissed it as “overkill,” despite the database system saying to use tables for “a list or log of their own kept for later” and memory guidance saying entries belong where entries are kept, not as individual memories. At step 15, it created another memory instead of correcting the existing one, contrary to the instruction, “Correct a memory the fact changes rather than keeping a second.” The date calculations and reminder limitation were handled correctly, but the information never became a structured maintenance log.

- `system-prompt` (0.91): The assistant missed the chance to ask for the missing date and start a reusable log, then treated a memory as a substitute for structured tracking even though the prompt describes these as different uses.
  > When a person says they have trouble remembering repeated events or wants to keep track of changes over time, treat that as a possible request for a log. If the starting date or other essential entry details are missing, ask for them and offer to start the log. For repeated entries, use a database table or another existing place that stores entries; a memory is for a lasting fact or preference, not a substitute for an entry in a log. Save the confirmed entry there, and use memory only for a separate lasting fact that will help in later chats. Do not create a log if the person only wants one fact remembered.
- `context:hub/remember` (0.84): The memory instructions say to correct changed facts rather than create a second memory, but the assistant called `hub__remember` again and left the old fact in place.
  > If a fact already has a memory and the person gives a correction or an updated value, update that memory with `hub__memory_update`; do not create a second memory for the same fact. Search for and load `hub__memory_update` if it is not among your tools. If the fact is also an entry in a structured log, update that entry as well.
- `system-prompt` (0.83): The final response called the information “Saved” without clarifying that only a memory had been saved, not the structured log the person needed.
  > When describing a save or change, name only the place the tool result confirms. Do not imply that information was added to a log, table, file, form, or other structured record unless a tool result confirms that change. If you saved only a memory, say that; if a requested structured record was not created or updated, say so plainly.

items.md:
**Request:** "Can you start keeping track of what I spend on groceries? My last trip was Kroger on Nov 14, $172.48." → "Here's my receipt, add it to what I spent." _[receipt]_

**Good:** Reads the store and total, adds it to the grocery log (seeded in the first step), asks if a category is unclear.

Mean 7.3/10 · same verdict every rep · $0.111

### rep 1: pass 7/10

The assistant read the receipt’s Kroger store, date, and total, then saved the purchase to the existing grocery log after the user confirmed. It added an unnecessary confirmation step even though the user had already asked it to add the receipt.

- ✓ Read the receipt details accurately
- ✓ Saved the purchase to the grocery log
- ✓ Did not claim it was saved before the database write
- ✗ Asked for confirmation before adding a receipt the user had already asked it to add

**Request:** "Help me plan my mom's 70th birthday party."

**Good:** Asks the few things that matter (date, how many, budget) in one go, then a plan and a checklist.

Mean 6.7/10 · verdicts differ · $0.223

### rep 1: pass 8/10

The assistant asked the key planning questions together, made a tailored plan, and ultimately provided a complete, printable checklist in the chat. The first checklist was only saved under a filename, so the user had to ask again to see it.

- ✓ Asked about the date, location, guest count, budget, and preferences in one go.
- ✓ Created a plan suited to a relaxed gathering, gardening, Italian food, and the stated budget.
- ✓ Saved the checklist and then showed it in the chat when the user couldn’t access the file.
- ✗ Initially gave only a filename instead of showing the checklist or explaining how to open it.

Cause **other**, layer **chat-prompt**. Fix: When creating a checklist, show its contents in the chat as well as saving it to a file.

4 turns · 4 runs · 8 model calls · hub $0.0186 · person $0.0011 · 57s · ended: satisfied (The checklist is now shown right in the chat where I can read and print it, which is exactly what I asked for.)

**Diagnosis:** The assistant correctly searched memory at step 1 and produced a useful plan, but at step 2 it chose a plain question even though `input__get_input` was available and the Forms guidance said to use a form for several details. At step 3 it did not apply the Memory guidance to the durable preference about a family member. The checklist problem arose at step 6: the core prompt says “boxes, a checklist or a table in it can't be ticked or changed and keep nothing, so never offer them as something to mark off,” which does not distinguish an interactive checklist from a printable paper checklist; the file guidance also says to tell the person the path without establishing that the path is user-accessible. The assistant eventually read and displayed the checklist, but at step 8 it added an unsupported claim about an app print option.

- `context:input/basics` (0.74): The guidance describes forms but did not lead the assistant to use one for a first round of several essential planning questions.
  > When you need several independent answers before you can give a useful recommendation or plan, use `input__get_input` to ask for the essentials together in one form. Do not ask the same set of questions as a plain text list unless the person prefers to answer in chat or a form would add unnecessary friction. Ask only what would materially change the first useful result; you can ask follow-up questions later. After showing the form, end your turn and use the answers when they arrive.
- `context:fs/guide` (0.80): The file guide says to inspect the served folders, but the assistant guessed a path without first checking the root.
  > Before choosing a file path, call `fs__list` on `.` to see the first served folder. Use a path inside a folder the file system serves; do not assume that a path or filename is available to the person just because `fs__write` can create it.

### rep 2: weak 6/10

The assistant gathered the key details in one form, remembered the allergy, and gave a useful dated party plan. But it never delivered a working in-app checklist, and its repeated database repair attempts took a long time before it settled on the typed schedule fallback.

- ✓ Asked for the date, location, guest count, budget, preferences, and must-haves together.
- ✓ Gave a practical budget and dated schedule, and clearly flagged the failed web search.
- ✓ Warned about peanut ingredients and cross-contact and remembered Leo’s allergy.
- ✓ Eventually stated plainly that no checklist tasks had been added.
- ✗ Initially implied the checklist was ready and tasks could be marked done before verifying that adding tasks worked.
- ✗ Spent many calls trying to repair database operations instead of quickly providing a checkable fallback in chat.
- ✗ Did not deliver the requested working check-off list.

Cause **tool-error**, layer **fn**. Fix: Verify that checklist entries can actually be saved before calling the checklist ready, and switch promptly to a clear checkbox-style fallback if the database write fails.

**Checks failed:** no-run-errors (6 of 69 tool calls failed or were refused: web/search (failed), database/get_query (failed), database/author_query (failed), use_saved (tool-error); apart: 9 model arg mistakes, 0 recovered, 9 not (the model's own call sent back to fix; not failures))

5 turns · 69 runs · 61 model calls · hub $0.135 · person $0.0016 · 279s · ended: satisfied (The in-app checklist plainly can't be created right now and the assistant was upfront about it, so the typed schedule is a fine fallback and I'm satisfied.)

**Diagnosis:** The main failure was in steps 28, 31, 49–50, and 52–59: the database authoring path rejected structured INSERTs with the misleading error “Received a prose query,” even though the agent’s instructions explicitly define an INSERT as structured JSON; an earlier accepted draft also failed at runtime with “no such function: make_date.” That left both the bulk insert and the one-item test unable to save tasks, so the assistant could not deliver a working check-off list. In step 44 it promised the person they would be able to mark items complete before verifying that adding and listing worked, contrary to the prompt’s instruction not to claim an action or result before the tools confirm it. The assistant eventually gave an honest schedule fallback, but repeated database retries prolonged the failure; steps 57 and 59 also ignored the authoring agent’s explicit instruction not to repeat the same draft.

- `hub-behaviour` (0.97): The database authoring and execution path rejected valid structured INSERT drafts as “Received a prose query,” and a draft that passed validation generated a date function unsupported by the database. The error “Describe what you want differently or more exactly” was not a useful remedy for a structured query that the checker misclassified.
  > Fix the database query authoring and execution path so a structured INSERT passed to the draft checker remains structured through validation, saving, and execution. Support the documented insert shape, including multiple rows, and bind date values using syntax supported by the active database dialect. Never report “Received a prose query” when the input is structured JSON. If a query cannot be supported, return an error that names the specific unsupported field or expression and a valid correction; do not advise the caller to rephrase a valid structured query.
- `system-prompt` (0.90): The prompt says “Never say something was saved, made, changed or done until a result says so” and instructs the assistant not to offer plain text as a checkable list. Nevertheless, the assistant said “you’ll be able to mark them done” before checking that the add, list, and update operations worked.
  > For any request to track items with a status, do not call the tracker ready or promise that the person can mark items complete until you have confirmed that at least one item was saved and that the available path for viewing or changing its status works. A created table or saved query alone does not prove the tracker works. If a write or verification fails, say exactly what failed and offer a clearly labeled text-only fallback; never describe plain text as interactive or checkable.
- `context:database/basics` (0.84): The database guidance describes making and regenerating saved queries, but does not give a stop rule for repeated authoring failures. The inner agent repeated the same structured INSERT after the same error, while the chat continued trying repairs after the list and refresh operations had already failed.
  > When a structured query is rejected, make at most one substantive correction based on the reported problem. Changing only the query’s name or description is not a correction. If the same error returns, stop authoring that query and tell the person what failed. For a requested tracker, do not keep regenerating or editing operations after the tool reports that they do not fit the table; use another available method only if its tool description and results show that it can actually complete the task.

**Request:** "What's going on this weekend near me?"

**Good:** Uses or asks for the location, real events with dates and links.

### rep 1: pass 7/10

The assistant asked for the missing location and family preferences, then clearly explained that search was blocked by a usage limit instead of inventing events. It couldn’t provide the requested events or links, but it was transparent about that limitation.

- ✗ Could have pointed more directly to a specific official Columbus events calendar.

Cause **tool-error**, layer **fn**. Fix: Restore web-search availability or provide a reliable fallback to official local event calendars when search is unavailable.

**Checks failed:** no-run-errors (2 of 6 tool calls failed or were refused: web/search (failed); apart: no model arg mistakes)

**Diagnosis:** The main failure was the search provider’s usage limit at steps 4 and 5, so the assistant could not retrieve or read event listings and had no verified events or links to offer. At step 5, the core instruction to “try at most one different approach” did not distinguish a recoverable search failure from an explicit provider quota limit, leading to another search against the same blocked service. - `hub-behaviour` (0.82): Web search failed with an explicit usage-limit error, leaving no results to read and no way in this run to retrieve current events or links.

If an independently configured search provider or reliable, maintained directory of official public calendars is available, use that fallback and cite the pages actually checked. Otherwise return the provider error to the assistant clearly and stop the search; do not fabricate results or links.
- `context:web/guide` (0.90): The general instruction to try another approach after a failed call can encourage repeating web searches even when the result explicitly says the provider’s usage limit has been reached.
  > If web__search reports a quota, usage-limit, or plan-limit error, do not retry web__search with a different query: the provider limit is not caused by the query. Use a genuinely independent source only if one is available and you can verify it. If not, say that current pages could not be checked and do not provide unverified event details or links.
- `context:hub/memory` (0.78): The instructions say to keep lasting preferences and relevant facts about who is around the person, but the assistant saved only the location after the person also gave a lasting preference relevant to future recommendations.
  > When a person shares more than one lasting fact that is likely to matter in later chats, keep each relevant fact as its own memory. items.md:
**Request:** "Help me write a nice note to my neighbor about their dog barking."

**Good:** A friendly draft, offers a firmer one; no tools needed.

Mean 8.0/10 · same verdict every rep · $0.0165

### rep 1: pass 8/10

The assistant produced a short, friendly note tailored with Dave’s and Bruno’s names and the specific morning hours. It didn’t offer a firmer alternative, but the note met the person’s stated goal.

- ✓ Personalized the note with the neighbor’s and dog’s names and the barking times
- ✓ Kept it brief, friendly, and suitable to leave on a door
- ✓ Used no tools
- ✗ Did not offer a firmer version

2 turns · 0 runs · 2 model calls · hub $0.0032 · person $0.0003 · 16s · ended: satisfied (The note is short, friendly, names Dave and Bruno, and mentions the morning times—exactly what I wanted to leave on his door.)

**Diagnosis:** Step 1 went well as a plain-chat writing task, but the prompt did not tell the model to offer a firmer alternative for this kind of note. At step 2, the model had the instruction “Say only what is true” and was told the barking hours, but not that it woke the person; it nevertheless added “often wakes me up.” The app terms and tools did not affect the outcome.

- `system-prompt` (0.90): The general instruction “Say only what is true” does not explicitly warn that a first-person draft must not invent the writer’s feelings, experiences, or consequences. The model added an unsupported personal impact at step 2.
  > When drafting words for the person to send or say, use only facts and personal experiences they have provided. Do not invent what they felt, noticed, experienced, or what happened as a result. If a useful detail is unknown, leave it out or use a clear placeholder. For example, do not write “This has caused me to miss meetings” unless the person said that happened.
- `system-prompt` (0.78): No instruction called for the optional firmer alternative the Good line expects, so the model gave only one version at both steps.
  > For a request to draft a message about a sensitive or potentially awkward concern, give the requested version first. When it would be useful, briefly offer a second version with a firmer tone, or ask whether the person would like one. Do not add extra versions when they would not help.

Do not add alternatives when the person asks for only one version or when they would distract from the request.

Use neutral wording instead, or ask if the detail is important. For example, write “I wanted to mention that I noticed…” rather than claiming “It has been keeping me up” unless the person said that.

### rep 1: pass 8/10

The assistant read the supplied page directly, saved the recipe and its instructions in the Household database, and updated the shopping list after the person shared what they already had. The search call failed, but reading the URL directly recovered the needed information.

- ✓ Saved the recipe with its source URL, servings, ingredients, and instructions.
- ✓ Provided a shopping list and removed pasta, salt, pepper, and olive oil when asked.
- ✗ The final list omitted quantities for butter and the seasonings.

**Checks failed:** no-run-errors (1 of 17 tool calls failed or were refused: web/search (failed); apart: no model arg mistakes)

2 turns · 17 runs · 12 model calls · hub $0.0267 · person $0.0005 · 63s · ended: satisfied (The recipe was saved and the shopping list was corrected to leave out items I already have.)

**Diagnosis:** The model handled persistence well: steps 5, 6, and 10 show it checked the database, created a suitable table, and confirmed the recipe was saved. At step 3, it searched even though the person supplied the exact page URL; the web guide's “web__search with a few key words” default did not make the direct-URL exception clear, and the search then failed with a usage-limit error. Reading the URL directly at step 4 recovered. The user-facing list issue came at steps 11 and 12: the saved recipe call at step 10 contained the quantities, but the assistant omitted them from both lists and deferred the spice amounts to the saved recipe. At step 1 it also skipped the memory search called for by the prompt when a personal list depends on what the person already has; the person supplied that information in the follow-up.

- `context:web/guide` (0.94): The guide says to search first, without distinguishing a request that already includes the exact page URL. This prompted an unnecessary search that failed even though the page could be read directly.
  > If the person gives you the exact URL of a page they want you to inspect, use web__read on that URL directly. Search first only when you need to find a page or need other sources. If a search fails but the person supplied a URL, try reading that URL directly before reporting that you could not get the information.
- `system-prompt` (0.83): The memory instructions say to search when an answer depends on personal information, but the model did not search memories before making a personal list.
  > Before making a list or recommendation that depends on the person's preferences, restrictions, or what they already have, check the memories available for relevant facts if none are already in front of you. Use relevant memories without asking the person to repeat them. Do not save temporary facts, such as a current inventory, as lasting memories unless the person asks you to remember them.
- `system-prompt` (0.96): The assistant left out quantities from a source-derived shopping list even though the saved recipe contained them, and repeated the omission after the person narrowed the list.
  > When you turn information from a source or saved record into a list, preserve useful quantities and units for each item whenever the source provides them. Do not omit available quantities by saying they are elsewhere. If a quantity is not given, do not invent one; leave it unquantified or say it was not specified.
